```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 6.5,
  fig.height = 5, dpi = 120, out.width = "100%", raster3d = 1e5, dev = "svglite",
  fig.ext = "svg", dev.args = list(pointsize = 14))
PAL <- c(blue = "#2E6F9E", red = "#B5342B", green = "#3F7A3D",
         orange = "#9E5E0F", purple = "#7A4F9E", teal = "#2A7A7A")
```

```{r packages, message=FALSE}
library(ggplot2)
library(ggplot3d)
theme_set(theme_minimal(base_size = 17) + theme(
  plot.background = element_rect(fill = "transparent", colour = NA),
  panel.background = element_rect(fill = "transparent", colour = NA),
  legend.background = element_rect(fill = "transparent", colour = NA),
  legend.position = "none"))
```

An implicit surface is the set of points where a function of x, y and z
takes one value. `geom_isofunction_3d()` samples the function on a grid over
the position scales, extracts the level set and then moves every vertex onto
the exact level along its grid edge, so a coarse grid still gives a surface
that lies on the function's zero set.

Point clouds can also supply a surface through an alpha shape or a fitted
implicit function. The reconstruction examples below use small samples;
installation is covered in [Get started](ggplot3d.html).

```{r box}
cube <- function(k) list(xlim(-k, k), ylim(-k, k), scale_z_continuous(limits = c(-k, k)))
```

## Algebraic surfaces

Barth's sextic has 65 ordinary double points, the most a sextic surface can
have. The polynomial below is the one of PyVista's contouring example; points
outside the sphere of radius sqrt(3.1) are set to `NA`, which masks their
grid cells.

```{r barth, fig.alt="Barth's sextic surface clipped to a sphere, with its repeated lobes and singular intersections."}
phi <- (1 + sqrt(5)) / 2
barth <- function(x, y, z) {
  x2 <- x^2; y2 <- y^2; z2 <- z^2
  v <- 3 * (phi^2 * x2 - y2) * (phi^2 * y2 - z2) * (phi^2 * z2 - x2) -
    (1 + 2 * phi) * (x2 + y2 + z2 - 1)^2
  ifelse(x2 + y2 + z2 > 3.1, NA, v)
}
ggplot() +
  geom_isofunction_3d(fun = barth, levels = 0, n = 48, fill = PAL[["blue"]]) +
  cube(1.8) + coord_3d()
```

The Clebsch diagonal cubic contains all 27 lines a smooth cubic surface can
carry, each one real.

```{r clebsch, fig.alt="The Clebsch diagonal cubic as an orange algebraic surface."}
clebsch <- function(x, y, z) {
  81 * (x^3 + y^3 + z^3) - 189 * (x^2 * (y + z) + y^2 * (z + x) + z^2 * (x + y)) +
    54 * x * y * z + 126 * (x * y + y * z + z * x) - 9 * (x^2 + y^2 + z^2) -
    9 * (x + y + z) + 1
}
ggplot() +
  geom_isofunction_3d(fun = clebsch, levels = 0, n = 40, fill = PAL[["orange"]]) +
  cube(1) + coord_3d()
```

## Triply periodic surfaces

The Schwarz P surface is close to the zero set of cos x + cos y + cos z. Two
level sets on either side of zero bound a wall around it.

```{r schwarz, fig.alt="Two level surfaces of the Schwarz P approximation surrounding its periodic openings."}
schwarz <- function(x, y, z) cos(x) + cos(y) + cos(z)
ggplot() +
  geom_isofunction_3d(aes(fill = after_stat(factor(level))),
    fun = schwarz, levels = c(-0.4, 0.4), n = 36) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = unname(PAL[c("teal", "purple")]), name = "level") +
  cube(pi) + coord_3d()
```

## Shapes from signed distance functions

A signed distance function is negative inside a shape, positive outside and
zero on its surface. `sdf_sphere()`, `sdf_box()`, `sdf_torus()`,
`sdf_capsule()`, `sdf_plane()`, `sdf_gyroid()` and `sdf_metaballs()` build
them, and `|`, `&`, `-`, `sdf_blend()`, `sdf_offset()`, `sdf_shell()` and
`sdf_transform()` combine them. The result is still a function of x, y and
z, so it goes straight into `geom_isofunction_3d()`, which extracts its zero
set by default and takes the normals from its exact gradient.

```{r csg, fig.alt="A rounded solid with three intersecting cylindrical passages through it."}
part <- sdf_box(size = c(2, 2, 2), radius = 0.15) & sdf_sphere(radius = 1.3)
drill <- sdf_capsule(c(-2, 0, 0), c(2, 0, 0), 0.5) |
  sdf_capsule(c(0, -2, 0), c(0, 2, 0), 0.5) |
  sdf_capsule(c(0, 0, -2), c(0, 0, 2), 0.5)
part - drill
ggplot() +
  geom_isofunction_3d(fun = part - drill, n = 40, fill = PAL[["green"]]) +
  cube(1.2) + coord_3d()
```

`sdf_blend()` replaces the sharp minimum of a union by a smooth one that adds
at most `k` where the shapes meet. A gyroid sheet cut by a sphere shows a
second use of the same algebra: `sdf_shell()` turns the gyroid's zero set
into a wall of given thickness.

```{r blend, fig.alt="A red gyroid sheet with finite thickness, cut to a spherical boundary."}
blob <- sdf_blend(sdf_sphere(c(-0.6, 0, 0), 0.6),
  sdf_torus(c(0.5, 0, 0), major = 0.6, minor = 0.2), k = 0.15)
sheet <- sdf_shell(sdf_gyroid(period = 1.2), 0.08) & sdf_sphere(radius = 1.2)
ggplot() +
  geom_isofunction_3d(fun = sheet, n = 56, fill = PAL[["red"]]) +
  cube(1.25) + coord_3d()
```

Because the expression tree of a distance function can also be evaluated on
whole boxes in interval arithmetic, `adaptive = TRUE` refines an octree only
near the surface and near its sharp edges.

```{r adaptive, fig.alt="A sphere smoothly joined to a torus, extracted with adaptive refinement."}
ggplot() +
  geom_isofunction_3d(fun = blob, adaptive = TRUE, depth = c(3, 6),
    fill = PAL[["purple"]]) +
  xlim(-1.3, 1.4) + ylim(-0.9, 0.9) + scale_z_continuous(limits = c(-0.7, 0.7)) +
  coord_3d()
```

## Scattered height measurements

A height surface has one height at each horizontal position. Sample 200
locations from the built-in volcano matrix and join their x/y positions
with a Delaunay triangulation. The triangles interpolate their three
measured heights; their edges are visible here to show the irregular mesh.

```{r scattered-heights, fig.alt="A triangular height surface reconstructed from 200 scattered volcano elevations, with mesh edges visible."}
terrain <- expand.grid(x = seq_len(nrow(volcano)), y = seq_len(ncol(volcano)))
terrain$z <- as.vector(volcano)
set.seed(12)
samples <- terrain[sample(seq_len(nrow(terrain)), 200), ]
ggplot(samples, aes(x, y, z = z)) +
  geom_surface_3d(method = "delaunay", fill = PAL["green"],
                   colour = "grey40", linewidth = 0.15) +
  coord_3d(aspect = c(1.4, 1, 0.7))
```

This surface ends at the convex hull of the sampled horizontal positions.
For an object with several surface heights at the same x/y position, use
three-dimensional reconstruction.

## Alpha shapes

An alpha shape selects local connections between points using a radius
threshold. Sample a torus with major radius 1 and tube radius 0.35. This
gives a point cloud whose reconstructed surface can retain a central hole.

```{r torus-sample}
set.seed(6)
u <- runif(400, 0, 2 * pi)
v <- runif(400, 0, 2 * pi)
torus <- data.frame(x = (1 + 0.35 * cos(v)) * cos(u),
                    y = (1 + 0.35 * cos(v)) * sin(u), z = 0.35 * sin(v))
shape <- ggplot(torus, aes(x, y, z = z))
```

The radius threshold uses transformed position units. A smaller threshold
can leave disconnected pieces, while a sufficiently large one fills the
convex hull. The opacity argument controls transparency independently of
the reconstruction radius.

```{r alpha-shape, fig.alt="An alpha-shape surface around sampled torus points, retaining the hole through its centre."}
shape + geom_alpha_shape_3d(radius = 0.4, fill = PAL["teal"], alpha = 0.7) +
  geom_point_3d(size = 0.4) + coord_3d(aspect = "data", elevation = 50)
```

```{r alpha-hull, fig.alt="The convex hull of the same torus sample, spanning the central hole."}
shape + geom_alpha_shape_3d(radius = Inf, fill = PAL["orange"]) +
  coord_3d(aspect = "data", elevation = 50)
```

With an automatic threshold, the stat chooses the smallest radius at which
the selected tetrahedra touch every point. See
[geom_alpha_shape_3d()](../reference/stat_alpha_shape_3d.html) for the
boundary triangles and computed variables.

## Fitting an implicit function to points

A radial basis function fit estimates a scalar field whose zero set passes
through the sample. It also constrains points a small distance to either
side of the surface, using supplied or estimated normals. The fit below
uses 80 sampled points on an ellipsoid with vertical semi-axis 0.6 and
supplies its analytical normal directions.

```{r reconstruction-data}
set.seed(2)
unit <- matrix(rnorm(240), ncol = 3)
unit <- unit / sqrt(rowSums(unit^2))
shell <- data.frame(x = unit[, 1], y = unit[, 2], z = 0.6 * unit[, 3])
shell$nx <- shell$x
shell$ny <- shell$y
shell$nz <- shell$z / 0.6^2
```

The grid resolution controls extraction of the fitted zero set. The
smoothing parameter controls the fit itself. A dense linear solve limits
this method to 2,000 input points; use a small representative sample.

```{r rbf-fit, fig.alt="A smooth blue surface fitted through 80 ellipsoid samples, shown with the input points."}
ggplot(shell, aes(x, y, z = z, nx = nx, ny = ny, nz = nz)) +
  stat_implicit_fit_3d(method = "rbf", n = 18,
                        fill = PAL["blue"], alpha = 0.65) +
  geom_point_3d(size = 0.7) + coord_3d(aspect = "data")
```

Omit the three normal mappings to estimate normals from neighbouring
points. The neighbourhood size and smoothing arguments are described in
[stat_implicit_fit_3d()](../reference/stat_implicit_fit_3d.html).
